segments.text:
The module comment. The module only reads files, and GB means 1e9 bytes. It names two kinds of rate, and the code below keeps them separate:
- **Part A** (binaries `bw_old` and `bw_new`): the rate is the csv column `aggregate_GBps`, as the binary printed it.
- **bwx runners** (`bwx12` and its older versions): this module computes the rate from the T rows (one row per thread). Each thread gives bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9. The values of all threads are added.
segments.heading: Module comment: inputs and the two kinds of rate

segments.text: Imports of the Python standard library. `sys.dont_write_bytecode = True`: Python writes no compiled copy (`.pyc` file) of the modules that are imported after this line.

- `S`: the folder of this file, the scratch folder of the rerun.
- `CRB`: three levels above `S`. Here the name means the project folder `crb`, not the machine.
- `R`: `crb/results`, the result folders that were copied back from the machine.
- `W15`, `K13`: the scratch folders of 2026-11-15 (script `rx.sh`) and of 2026-11-13 (benchmark sources).
- `DIMM_REPORT`: the report on the memory modules, `machines/arm-crb/DIMM-flaky-report.md`, three levels above `crb`.
segments.heading: Folder paths, derived from the place of this file

segments.text: `sys.path.insert(0, S)` makes Python search the folder `S` first when it imports a module. The next two lines import the two quick statistics scripts of that folder. This module uses `stat_k120.HDR`, the pattern of a part A header line, in `read_k120` (line 271). `build_facts.py` also calls both scripts through this module to cross-check the numbers [Ref3].

`OPENED` is the list of the files that this module opened, in order, each path once. `_open` adds the absolute path to the list and then opens the file. Every reader below opens its file through `_open`. `facts_text.py` stops the script when the file list of the facts sheet does not name every file of `OPENED` [Ref4].
segments.heading: Function `_open`: open a file and record its path

segments.text: Shortens a path for the facts sheet. A path under the results folder becomes `R/...`. A path under the scratch folder becomes `S/...`. Any other path is returned as an absolute path.
segments.heading: Function `rel`: short path for the facts sheet

segments.text: Returns the SHA-256 checksum of a file as 64 hexadecimal digits.
segments.heading: Function `sha256`: checksum of a file

segments.text: Reads the date and time from the name of a result folder. Example: `k120-T72A1-20261117T221209Z` gives 2026-11-17 22:12:09. `ra.sh` and `rx.sh` put the UTC time at which they create the folder into its name [Ref5] [Ref6].
segments.heading: Function `folder_date`: time in a folder name

segments.text: Turns a time of day `HH:MM:SS` from a run file into a full date and time. The date comes from the folder name. When the result lies more than 1 s before the time of the folder name, one day is added. That is the case of a run that passed midnight.
segments.heading: Function `clock`: time of day to full date and time

segments.text:
`STATE` is the pattern (regular expression) of one state line. `go.sh` and `go2.sh` print state lines at the start, around the run steps and at the end [Ref7]. The fields of the line, in order:
- a label, the UTC time and the boot id.
- `MemTotal` in kB.
- the five fields of `/proc/loadavg`.
- `users`: the number of logins.
- `marker`: `present` or `absent`. It says whether the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING` existed.
- the number of processes per user.
segments.heading: Readers of logs and state files

segments.text:
Reads the log line by line and keeps every line in `lines`. A state line becomes one entry in `states`:
- `label`: for example `start`, `after T72A1` or `idle before T72I1`.
- `utc`, `boot`, `memtotal_kB`.
- `load1`, `load5`, `load15`: the load averages over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
- `runnable`, `tasks`: the tasks that are runnable now, and the number of all tasks.
- `logins`, `marker`, and `procs` (user name to number of processes).
- `line`: the line number in the log. The fifth field of `/proc/loadavg` (the id of the newest process) is matched and not stored.
segments.heading: Function `read_log`: log of `go.sh` or `go2.sh`

segments.text:
The other lines of the log:
- `== cmdline`, `== governors`, `== thp`, `== affinity`: the text and the line number go to `other`. These four lines hold the Linux boot arguments, the CPU frequency governors, the huge-page setting and the CPU list of the shell. Only `go.sh` prints them.
- The line `ALLDONE` sets `alldone` to true. `go.sh` and `go2.sh` print it as their last line.
- A line that starts with `FAILED` is added to `failed`. The two scripts print such a line when a check or a run step fails.

Reads the file `probe.txt` that `ra.sh` writes into a part A folder [Ref5]. It returns:
- `utc`, `load_before`, `logins`, `name`: the time, the three load averages, the number of logins and the name of the step, read directly before the first process.
- `boot`, `memtotal_kB`, `runnable`: the boot id, `MemTotal` and the number of runnable tasks. `ra.sh` reads this number in its wait loop, 5 s or more before the time `utc` [Ref5].
- `kernel`: the Linux kernel release. `thp`: the huge-page setting of Linux.
- `load_after`, `utc_after`, `memtotal_after_kB`: read after the last process.
- `sha`: file name to SHA-256 checksum, for `bw_old`, `bw_new` and `ra.sh`.
- `pcpu_max`: the highest %CPU value of the process list in the file.
segments.heading: Function `read_probe`: `probe.txt` of a part A folder

segments.text:
The patterns of the two line kinds of `launches.txt` [Ref6].
- `rx.sh` writes a `launch` line directly before it starts a process: tag, time of day, the five fields of `/proc/loadavg`, number of logins, arguments of the binary. The tag is the first field of the spec line, for example `a6456`.
- It writes an `rc` line when the process has ended: exit status, tag, time of day.

Returns one entry per `launch` line: tag, launch time (through `clock`), the three load averages, the runnable tasks, the number of all tasks, the logins, the arguments and the line number. An `rc` line fills `rc` (the exit status, kept as text) and `rc_utc` of the first entry with the same tag that has no exit status yet.
segments.heading: Function `read_launches`: `launches.txt` of `rx.sh`

segments.text:
`rx.sh` writes `env.txt` once, before its first process [Ref6]. The function returns:
- `start`: line 1, the date and time.
- `kernel`: line 2, the Linux kernel release.
- `loadavg`: line 3, the content of `/proc/loadavg`, as text.
- `binary`, `sha`: the path and the SHA-256 checksum of the runner, from the last line of the form `binary PATH CHECKSUM`. Both are `None` when the file has no such line.
- `top`: the rows of the process list after line 3, as (user, %CPU, command, line number). `pcpu_max` is the highest %CPU value.
- `n_lines`: the number of lines of the file.
segments.heading: Function `read_env`: `env.txt` of `rx.sh`

segments.text: Reads a saved text copy of the journal. It uses only lines that carry `{N}[Hardware Error]:`, where N is the record number. A line whose text starts with `Hardware error from APEI` opens a new record with its line number, its time and N. The first later line `event severity: ...` with the same N gives the severity of that record, for example `corrected`.
segments.heading: Function `read_error_records`: hardware error records of a journal

segments.text: Returns one entry per line that matches `HDR_STEP` (line 260): line number, tag, binary, kernel name (the word after `--kernel` in the arguments), launch time, arguments, 1-minute load average and step name. The csv files of the rerun of 2026-11-17 have no `-- step` line. `build_facts.py` calls this function for csv files of the earlier script `run_partA.sh`.
segments.heading: Function `step_headers`: `-- step` lines of an earlier csv

segments.text:
Reads `R/dimm7200-20261117/try6.txt`, the record of the memory modules in the boot of the rerun. Line 1 gives the time and line 2 gives the boot id. The loop finds four more values, each with its line number:
- `memtotal_kB`: `MemTotal` in kB.
- `dimm_sockets`: the number in the Linux kernel message `This system has N DIMM sockets`.
- `speed_count`, `speed_MTps`: the leading count and the speed of the line `12 Configured Memory Speed: 7200 MT/s`.
- `hwerr`: the number after `hwerr=`.
segments.heading: Function `read_try6`: record of 12 modules at 7200 MT/s

segments.text:
Checks `boots.txt` of the same folder. That file lists the boots of the journal, one per row: boot number, boot id, first time, last time.
- Exactly one row must have the number 0. Its boot id must equal the boot id of `try6.txt`, compared without the `-` characters.
- That row must have 10 fields, with `UTC` as field 6 and field 10.
- When one of these tests fails, the script stops with an error.
- `boots_first` and `boots_last` are the two times of that row.

Reads `gaps.txt` of the same folder. The row that starts with `0 first=` gives the first and the last time of the Linux kernel log of this boot, a DIMM count and a `hwerr` count. The lines after that row are the output of `uptime` and a process list. The function stores the time of the `uptime` line (with the date of the first log time) and the rows of the process list as (user, %CPU, command, line number).

`HDR_STEP` is the pattern of a `-- step` header line. The earlier scripts `run_partA.sh` and `run_bwx.sh` wrote such a line as the header of each process. `ra.sh` and `rx.sh` of the rerun do not write this form. The fields of the line, in order:
- step, tag and binary.
- the wait time (`waited_s`).
- the three load averages, the runnable tasks and the number of all tasks.
- the logins, the time of day and the arguments of the binary.
segments.heading: Part A files: csv of `bw_old` and `bw_new`

segments.text:
Reads a part A csv such as `threads120.csv` line by line. A line that matches `stat_k120.HDR` (`-- binary ...`) starts a new process. `ra.sh` writes this line directly before it starts the binary [Ref5]. The entry holds:
- `binary`: `bw_old` or `bw_new`. `kernel`: the kernel name. With the kernel `read`, `bw_old` is the old read kernel and `bw_new` is the new read kernel.
- `round`: the round of the script (1 or 2).
- `load1`: the 1-minute load average at launch. `utc`: the time of day.
- `hdr_threads`, `hdr_cpus`, `hdr_bytes`: thread count, CPU list and buffer size of the header line, as text.
- `iv`: the list of intervals, empty at first.
segments.heading: Function `read_k120`: processes and intervals of a part A csv

segments.text:
The header form of the earlier script `run_partA.sh`. The csv files of the rerun have no such header.
- The kernel name is the word after `--kernel` in the arguments.
- The round is the number at the end of the tag.
- When the caller passes a test function `only_tags`, a process whose tag fails the test is not added to the result. The interval rows after it are then dropped with it.

The comment line that the binary prints first. `copy_note` records whether the line holds the text `copy counts read+write bytes`. The text means that the binary counts the bytes read plus the bytes written for the kernels `copy` and `asmcopy` [Ref1]. `bw_hdr` keeps the last part of the line: threads, bytes per thread, `min_ms` (the shortest length of one interval in ms) and `thp`.

Splits the line at the commas. A row with 6 fields that starts with `thread` is a per-thread row of the option `--per-thread`. Its rate (field 6, GB/s) is stored per repetition in `thr`. The csv files of the rerun hold no such row: `ra.sh` does not pass `--per-thread` [Ref5].

**Which rows count as interval rows.** A row after a header line is an interval row when it has at least 10 fields and its field 4 (`rep`) is a number. This test leaves out the column title row and the `best` row. The script stops with an error when field 1 (the kernel name) differs from the kernel of the header line before it, unless that header says `all`.

**The part A rate.** Each interval row becomes one entry in `iv`. No value is computed again here, except `passes`:
- `agg` = field 7, `aggregate_GBps`. This is the rate of the interval. The binary computed it as the sum of the bytes of all threads / the longest per-thread time / 1e9, and printed it with 2 decimals [Ref1].
- `total_bytes` = field 5. `elapsed_s` = field 6, the longest per-thread time in seconds.
- `tmin`, `tmax`, `tavg` = fields 8, 9, 10: the lowest, highest and mean per-thread rate in GB/s.
- `passes` = field 5 / field 3 (`bytes_per_thread`), rounded down.
- `rep`, `threads`, `kernel` and the line number of the row.
- Example: the first interval row of `threads120.csv` of T72A1 is `read,120,268435456,0,256087425024,0.5474,467.83,2.98,4.93,3.99`. It gives `agg` = 467.83 GB/s and `passes` = 954 [Ref9].

Returns an empty container for the rows of one process:
- `step`, `step_line`: the values and the line number of the `-- step` header line, if the file has one.
- `hdr`: the values of the comment lines at the top of the csv.
- `T`: the T rows. `Tl`: the line range of the T rows.
- `I`: the I rows. `P`: the P rows. `C`: the number of C rows.
segments.heading: bwx csv files. Function `_new_section`: empty container for one process

segments.text:
Reads the csv of a runner, for example `a6456.csv` (part L, control I) or `cfwd.csv` and `crev.csv` (part C).
- A csv that `rx.sh` wrote has no `-- step` line. The whole file is then one section, and it holds one process.
- A csv of the earlier script `run_bwx.sh` has one `-- step` line per process. Each such line starts a new section and its values are stored in `step`.
segments.heading: Function `read_bwx`: rows of a bwx csv

segments.text:
Comment lines start with `#`.
- From the lines `# bandwidth:` and `# bwx:` the function stores 8 values in `hdr`, as text: `min_ms`, `thp`, `seq`, `rounds`, `stop`, `start`, `two_buffers`, `count`. The first value found is kept.
- `seq` is the kernel sequence of the process, for example `oldread,asmread,read_nop96,read_nop256,read_1pl`.
- `stop` is the stop rule [Ref2]. `common`: the runner sets one start time and one deadline, `min_ms` milliseconds later, for all threads. Each thread stops after the chunk (2 MiB here) in which the deadline passes. `pass`: each thread stops after a whole pass over its buffer, `min_ms` milliseconds or more after its own start.
- `start` is not a time. It is the place in its buffer where a thread starts: `common` (the start of the buffer) or `offset` (a 2 MiB chunk that depends on the thread number) [Ref2].
- All 9 bwx12 csv files of the rerun (parts L and C, control I) say `stop=common` and `start=common`.
- Every other comment line is skipped, for example the column title lines and the `# page_read` lines.

**T rows: one row per thread and interval.** A T row must have 13 fields, or the script stops. The key of an interval is (round, pos, kernel name), from fields 2 to 4. For each thread 6 values are kept [Ref2]:
- `cpu` = field 6: the CPU of the thread.
- `bytes` = field 7: the bytes that the runner counted for this thread in the interval. For a read kernel it adds the size of every buffer range that it gave to the kernel. `oldread`, `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop256` read every byte of the range. `read_1pl` loads only 16 of every 64 bytes, and the runner still counts the full size.
- `elapsed_s` = field 8: the time of this thread in seconds, printed with 6 decimals. It runs from the clock read directly before the first timed kernel call of the thread to the clock read after its last kernel call. The warm-up call of the interval comes before this time.
- flags = field 13: `late` or `-`.
- `t_start_s`, `t_end_s` = fields 10 and 11: the start and the end of the time `elapsed_s` of this thread, in seconds since the process start.
- `Tl` keeps the first and the last line number of the T rows of each interval. Fields 5, 9 and 12 (`tid`, `t_sched_s`, `passes`) are not kept.

**I rows: one row per interval.** Stored under the same key: `threads` = field 6, `total_bytes` = field 7, `max_elapsed_s` = field 8, `agg` = field 9 and the line number. `agg` is `aggregate_GBps` as the runner printed it: total bytes / longest per-thread time, with 2 decimals [Ref2]. This module does not use `agg` as the rate of the interval. `build_facts.py` checks that it differs from the total of the T rows by less than 0.05 GB/s [Ref3].

- A P row holds the page state of one buffer. It is stored as a tuple: round, pos, thread, buffer letter and the 6 numbers of fields 6 to 11 (the first two are `kB_total` and `kB_huge`). The buffer letter is `a` for the first buffer of a thread and `b` for its second buffer. The 9 bwx12 csv files of the rerun hold only `a` rows.
- C rows hold counter values. They are only counted.
- A row of any other kind is ignored.

Takes one section and returns one entry per interval, in file order. `seq` is the kernel sequence of the header, as a list of names. For each interval `tl` is the list of its T rows, one per thread.
- `rate`: bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9 of one thread, in GB/s. Each thread is divided by its own time.
- `m0`: the rates of the threads on CPUs 0 to 63 (mesh 0).
- `m1`: the rates of the threads on CPUs 64 and higher (mesh 1).
- No T row is left out. A row with the flag `late` is used like every other row. The 9 bwx12 csv files of the rerun hold no row with this flag.
segments.heading: Function `bwx_intervals`: one rate per interval from the T rows

segments.text:
- `i` is the I row of the same interval, or `None` when the file has none.
- `before` is the kernel that was timed directly before this interval in the same process. For a position above 0 it is the kernel one position earlier in `seq`. For position 0 of a later round it is the last kernel of `seq`. For the first interval of the process it is `None`.
- The value comes from `seq`, not from a time in the file. Before each timed interval the runner also makes one warm-up pass with the kernel of that interval. This pass is not timed [Ref2].
- The `assert` stops the script when the kernel name of the rows is not the name at this position of `seq`.

**The bwx rate.**
- `total` = sum of `m0` + sum of `m1`: the sum of the per-thread rates of all threads of the interval, in GB/s. `build_facts.py` takes this value as the rate of a bwx12 interval [Ref3].
- `mesh0`, `mesh1`: the same sum for each mesh. `threads`: the number of T rows of the interval. `n0`, `n1`: the thread counts per mesh.
- `m0_min` to `m1_max`: the lowest and the highest per-thread rate of each mesh.
- `is_64_56`: true when 64 threads ran on CPUs 0 to 63 and 56 threads on CPUs 64 to 119, on 120 different CPUs.
- Nothing is rounded here.
- Example: T72L1, `a6456.csv`, round 0, position 0, `oldread`. The 120 T rows give 305.13 GB/s on mesh 0 and 157.17 GB/s on mesh 1. Their sum `total` is 462.30 GB/s. The I row says 462.29 GB/s [Ref8].

The other values of the entry:
- `flagged`: the number of T rows whose flag is not `-`. `flags`: the different flag values of the interval.
- `I_agg`, `line`, `max_elapsed_s`: taken from the I row. `line` is the line number of the I row. All three are `None` when the interval has no I row.
- `t_start`: the earliest `t_start_s` of the T rows of the interval. `t_end`: the latest `t_end_s`. Both are in seconds since the process start.
- `T_first`, `T_last`: the first and the last line number of the T rows.

The result folders of the rerun, as (tag, number). The tag is the name that `go.sh` or `go2.sh` gave to the run script. It is part of the folder name.
- `RERUN_A`: part A, sessions 1 to 3.
- `RERUN_L`: part L, sessions 1 to 3.
- `RERUN_C`: part C, with the name of the spec file as third value. `T72C4` has no session (`None`): it ran after session 3.
- `RERUN_I`: control I. Its number counts the control processes. It is not a session.
segments.heading: The data sets of the rerun

segments.text: Short names of five binaries, each found by the first 8 hexadecimal digits of its SHA-256 checksum.

Returns the one folder under `R` whose name starts with the prefix followed by `-2026`. Example: `k120-T72A1` gives `R/k120-T72A1-20261117T221209Z`. The script stops with an error when it finds no folder or more than one.
segments.heading: Function `find`: result folder of a tag

segments.text:
Reads two things from the tables of `DIMM-flaky-report.md`. `build_facts.py` uses the table for the result folders of earlier runs [Ref3].
- A table row with a boot number, a start time and a module count gives one boot. The count may be written in bold.
- The row `Memory speed until ... UTC | N MT/s` gives the time until which the memory speed setting was N MT/s.
- The boots are returned in the order of their start time.
segments.heading: Function `read_boot_table`: boot history of the DIMM report

segments.text:
Returns a record with 40 keys. `build_facts.py` creates one record per interval [Ref3].
- Each key is `None` unless the caller passes a value.
- A key that is not in the list stops the script.
- The rate goes into `GBps`, and `rate_kind` says how the rate was formed.
segments.heading: Function `base_record`: one interval record of `facts.json`

segments.text: The two texts for `rate_kind`. `KIND_A` marks a part A record: the rate is the csv column `aggregate_GBps`. `KIND_X` marks a record of a bwx runner: the rate is the sum over the T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9.

Returns the records that pass every condition. A condition is written `key=value`.
- A plain value must be equal to the value of the record.
- A set, list or tuple must contain the value of the record.
- A function must return true for the value of the record.
- Example of a call in `facts_text.py`: `sel(recs, dataset='rerun-L', kernel='oldread')` returns the part L intervals of the old read kernel [Ref4].
segments.heading: Selection and statistics. Function `sel`: records that match conditions

segments.text:
Summarises a list of records, by default over the key `GBps`. An empty list gives `None`.
- `lo`, `hi`: the lowest and the highest value.
- `med`: the median. For an even number of values it is the mean of the two middle values.
- `n`: the number of records, that is the number of intervals.
- `procs`: the number of different processes (key `proc_key`).
- `sessions`: the number of different values of the key `session`. A record without a value is not counted. In a control I record the key holds the number of the control process, and `rng` counts it like a session. `boots`: the number of different boots.
- No value is left out and nothing is rounded. The function forms no mean over all values. The facts sheet prints a result as `lo` to `hi` with these counts [Ref4].
segments.heading: Function `rng`: lowest, highest, median and counts

segments.text: True when the two ranges share at least one value. Two ranges that only touch at one end count as overlapping. The function `compare` of `facts_text.py` sets the wording "no difference seen" when the 7200 MT/s range and the 8000 MT/s range overlap. It sets "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" when they do not [Ref4].
segments.heading: Function `overlap`: do two ranges share a value

segments.text: Gives the distance between the nearest ends of two ranges, in GB/s. The value is positive when range `a` lies fully above range `b`. It is negative when `a` lies fully below `b`. It is 0.0 when the ranges overlap.
segments.heading: Function `gap`: distance between two ranges

segments.text: Gives the width of a range in percent of its lower end: (`hi` - `lo`) / `lo` x 100.
segments.heading: Function `width_pct`: width of a range in percent
